scenes.tts: Four drugs act on one transmitter, with opposite effects. What decides which way each one pushes?
scenes.visual: Title fades. Four drug icons circle a single synapse labelled GABA, two arrows pointing up and down. The question appears beside them.
scenes.narration: Four drugs act on one transmitter, with opposite effects. What decides which way each one pushes?

scenes.tts: In 1921, Otto Lurvee reported slowing a frog heart by stimulating its vagus nerve.
scenes.caption: In 1921, Otto Loewi reported slowing a frog heart by stimulating its vagus nerve.
scenes.visual: A frog heart beats in a dish of salt solution, its vagus nerve attached. A stimulator sparks; the beat slows. Label: 1921, Otto Loewi.
scenes.narration: In 1921, Otto Loewi reported slowing a frog heart by stimulating its vagus nerve.

scenes.tts: He moved the fluid around it onto a second heart, and that heart slowed too.
scenes.visual: Fluid drips from the first dish into a second dish holding another beating heart. The second heart's beat slows.
scenes.narration: He moved the fluid around it onto a second heart, and that heart slowed too.

scenes.tts: Its own nerve was untouched. The first nerve had released a chemical.
scenes.visual: The second heart's untouched vagus is highlighted. A card: the message is a chemical.
scenes.narration: Its own nerve was untouched. The first nerve had released a chemical.

scenes.tts: If the message is a chemical, a drug can imitate it, block it, or make it last.
scenes.visual: Three small icons appear in turn: a copy, a block, an hourglass. Labels: imitate, block, make it last.
scenes.narration: If the message is a chemical, a drug can imitate it, block it, or make it last.

scenes.tts: Follow one molecule across a synapse. Three things happen to it.
scenes.visual: A schematic synapse draws: a nerve terminal above, a cleft, a target cell below. One glowing molecule sits in a vesicle.
scenes.narration: Follow one molecule across a synapse. Three things happen to it.

scenes.tts: First, it is released from the terminal, mostly when a spike arrives.
scenes.visual: A spike runs down the axon; the vesicle fuses and the molecule enters the cleft. Slot label stays on screen: 1 Released (source).
scenes.narration: First, it is released from the terminal, mostly when a spike arrives.

scenes.tts: Second, it is read by a receptor, a protein on the target cell.
scenes.visual: The molecule docks on a receptor in the target membrane. Slot label: 2 Read (readers).
scenes.narration: Second, it is read by a receptor, a protein on the target cell.

scenes.tts: Some receptors are ion channels that open within milliseconds.
scenes.visual: The receptor splits into two icons. Left: a channel opens and ions stream through. Label: ionotropic, milliseconds.
scenes.narration: Some receptors are ion channels that open within milliseconds.

scenes.tts: Others are G protein coupled receptors. They act through messengers inside the cell, over tens of milliseconds to minutes.
scenes.caption: Others are G-protein-coupled receptors. They act through messengers inside the cell, over tens of milliseconds to minutes.
scenes.visual: Right icon: a receptor with no pore triggers a cascade of messenger dots inside the cell. Label: metabotropic, GPCR, tens of milliseconds to minutes.
scenes.narration: Others are G-protein-coupled receptors. They act through messengers inside the cell, over tens of milliseconds to minutes.

scenes.tts: Third, it is removed, by an enzyme or by a transporter that pulls it back into a cell.
scenes.visual: In the cleft, an enzyme snips one molecule; a transporter in the terminal membrane pulls another back inside. Slot label: 3 Removed (off switch).
scenes.narration: Third, it is removed, by an enzyme or by a transporter that pulls it back into a cell.

scenes.tts: Source, readers, off switch. Every transmitter fills these three slots.
scenes.visual: The three slot labels line up in a row as a card: source, readers, off switch.
scenes.narration: Source, readers, off switch. Every transmitter fills these three slots.

scenes.tts: Think of a key, a lock, and a cleaner that sweeps keys away.
scenes.visual: The synapse becomes a lock-and-key cartoon: a key, a lock on the target cell, a small broom sweeping keys.
scenes.narration: Think of a key, a lock, and a cleaner that sweeps keys away.

scenes.tts: A copy of the key that turns the lock is an agonist.
scenes.visual: A second key, a different colour, enters the lock and turns it. Label: agonist.
scenes.narration: A copy of the key that turns the lock is an agonist.

scenes.tts: A key that fits but will not turn is a competitive antagonist.
scenes.visual: A blank key fills the lock and stays still; the real key bounces off. Label: competitive antagonist.
scenes.narration: A key that fits but will not turn is a competitive antagonist.

scenes.tts: Oil in the lock, so the real key turns more easily, is a positive allosteric modulator.
scenes.visual: A drop of oil lands on the side of the lock; the real key turns more easily. Label: positive allosteric modulator.
scenes.narration: Oil in the lock, so the real key turns more easily, is a positive allosteric modulator.

scenes.tts: Stopping the cleaner is a reuptake blocker or an enzyme inhibitor.
scenes.visual: The broom freezes; keys pile up and keep turning locks. Label: reuptake blocker or enzyme inhibitor.
scenes.narration: Stopping the cleaner is a reuptake blocker or an enzyme inhibitor.

scenes.tts: Gabba is the brain's main fast inhibitory transmitter. Here are four drugs that act on its system.
scenes.caption: GABA is the brain's main fast inhibitory transmitter. Here are four drugs that act on its system.
scenes.visual: A GABA synapse with its three slots labelled. GABA-A (channel) and GABA-B (GPCR) receptors sit on the target cell; a GABA transporter sits in the membrane.
scenes.narration: GABA is the brain's main fast inhibitory transmitter. Here are four drugs that act on its system.

scenes.tts: Baclofen activates gabba B receptors. Bicuculline sits in the gabba site of gabba A, without opening it.
scenes.caption: Baclofen activates GABA-B receptors. Bicuculline sits in the GABA site of GABA-A, without opening it.
scenes.visual: Two drug icons dock: baclofen on GABA-B, bicuculline in the GABA site of GABA-A.
scenes.narration: Baclofen activates GABA-B receptors. Bicuculline sits in the GABA site of GABA-A, without opening it.

scenes.tts: Diazepam binds a different site on gabba A and strengthens gabba's effect. Tiagabine blocks gat one, a gabba transporter.
scenes.caption: Diazepam binds a different site on GABA-A and strengthens GABA's effect. Tiagabine blocks GAT1, a GABA transporter.
scenes.visual: A diazepam icon docks at a separate site on the side of GABA-A; a tiagabine icon plugs the GABA transporter, labelled GAT1.
scenes.narration: Diazepam binds a different site on GABA-A and strengthens GABA's effect. Tiagabine blocks GAT1, a GABA transporter.

scenes.tts: Picture the receiving cell at a mature synapse, where gabba inhibits. Which drugs make inhibition stronger, and which weaker?
scenes.visual: All four icons in place. A small label on the target cell: mature synapse, GABA inhibits. On screen: Stronger or weaker? A five-second countdown ring.
scenes.narration: Picture the receiving cell at a mature synapse, where GABA inhibits. Which drugs make inhibition stronger, and which weaker?
scenes.caption: Picture the receiving cell at a mature synapse, where GABA inhibits. Which drugs make inhibition stronger, and which weaker?

scenes.tts: Baclofen, diazepam and tiagabine make it stronger. Bicuculline weakens it, and in animals it causes seizures. On terminals, baclofen can also cut gabba release, so circuits can differ.
scenes.visual: Baclofen, diazepam and tiagabine light up green with up arrows; bicuculline lights up red with a down arrow. Small note: model: receiving cell, mature synapse.
scenes.narration: Baclofen, diazepam and tiagabine make it stronger. Bicuculline weakens it, and in animals it causes seizures. On terminals, baclofen can also cut GABA release, so circuits can differ.
scenes.caption: Baclofen, diazepam and tiagabine make it stronger. Bicuculline weakens it, and in animals it causes seizures. On terminals, baclofen can also cut GABA release, so circuits can differ.

scenes.tts: Same transmitter, opposite effects. What decides is which step a drug changes, and in which direction.
scenes.visual: Baclofen, bicuculline and diazepam slide onto the reading slot and tiagabine onto removal, each with its arrow. The release slot stays empty.
scenes.narration: Same transmitter, opposite effects. What decides is which step a drug changes, and in which direction.

scenes.tts: The idea: classify a drug by the main step it changes. Release, reading, or removal.
scenes.visual: An idea card builds line by line. Line 1: Classify a drug by the main step it changes: release, reading or removal.
scenes.narration: The idea: classify a drug by the main step it changes. Release, reading, or removal.

scenes.tts: How much it changes that step depends on how much of its target it fills.
scenes.visual: Line 2 adds: How much depends on how much of its target it fills.
scenes.narration: How much it changes that step depends on how much of its target it fills.

scenes.tts: What that does to a disease is a separate question.
scenes.visual: Line 3 adds: What it does to a disease is a separate question.
scenes.narration: What that does to a disease is a separate question.

scenes.tts: The takeaway: find the step a drug changes, and the direction it pushes.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: Find the step, and the direction. Below, smaller: Next: how much a drug changes a step.
scenes.narration: The takeaway: find the step a drug changes, and the direction it pushes.
